title: For a given number N, generate all combinations of N pairs of balanced parentheses. Explain the backtracking technique that tracks open and close counts to keep every prefix valid.

s1_definition.profdef: Balanced Parentheses generates all valid strings of N open and N close parentheses using backtracking. We build the string character by character, tracking how many open and close parentheses have been placed. We may place an open parenthesis while fewer than N opens have been used, and a close parenthesis only while closes are fewer than opens, which guarantees every prefix stays valid. The number of results is the Nth Catalan number.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, nested approval brackets must open and close in balance, like opening a sub-approval only inside an open parent approval and closing children before parents. For N levels we want every valid bracketing. We build left to right: we can open a new bracket as long as we have brackets left to open, and we can close one only if there is an unclosed bracket waiting, which keeps the structure valid at every step.
s1_definition.oneliner: Backtrack placing an open while opens are below N, and a close only while closes trail opens.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Balanced Parentheses generates all valid strings of N open and N close parentheses using backtracking. We build the string character by character, tracking how many open and close parentheses have been placed. We may place an open parenthesis while fewer than N opens have been used, and a close parenthesis only while closes are fewer than opens, which guarantees every prefix stays valid. The number of results is the Nth Catalan number.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, nested approval brackets must open and close in balance, like opening a sub-approval only inside an open parent approval and closing children before parents. For N levels we want every valid bracketing. We build left to right: we can open a new bracket as long as we have brackets left to open, and we can close one only if there is an unclosed bracket waiting, which keeps the structure valid at every step.

**One line to remember:** Backtrack placing an open while opens are below N, and a close only while closes trail opens.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with two counters, `openCount` and `closeCount`, and a builder for the current string. If `openCount < n` we may append an open parenthesis and recurse with `openCount + 1`. If `closeCount < openCount` we may append a close parenthesis and recurse with `closeCount + 1`. When the string length reaches two times N it is a complete valid combination and we record it.

The close rule, `closeCount < openCount`, is the key invariant: a close is only legal when there is an unmatched open before it, so no prefix ever has more closes than opens. Backtracking undoes the last character after each recursive branch, for example by trimming the builder back to its previous length.

A senior-level nuance is that this generate-and-prune avoids ever building an invalid prefix, so unlike filtering all two-to-the-two-N strings it does no wasted work on invalid candidates. Another nuance is that the count of valid combinations is the Catalan number, which grows fast, so N must be modest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models nested approval structures where a sub-approval can only exist inside an open parent approval, and all children must close before their parent. For N approval levels the governance team wants every valid nesting to review possible workflows. This is exactly how Balanced Parentheses works: an open is a parent approval opening and a close is one closing.

Problem 2 — Enumerating structures and then checking validity wastes effort on invalid ones. This is why we backtrack with open and close counts so every string we build is valid by construction, never producing a broken nesting.

The code defines a `ParenthesesService` exposing `allBalanced(n)` returning the valid strings. A `Demo` runs it for N equal to two and logs the two valid combinations.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: N equal to two.

Step 1: Start empty with zero opens and zero closes. Opens are below two, so append an open. The string is "(" with one open.

Step 2: Opens are below two, so append another open. The string is "((" with two opens. Opens are no longer below two, so we cannot open more; closes are below opens, so append a close, giving "(()".

Step 3: Closes are still below opens, so append another close, giving "(())". The length is four, which is two times N, so store "(())". Backtrack.

Step 4: Return to the state "(" with one open, and this time append a close, giving "()". Then opens are below two, append an open, giving "()(", then a close, giving "()()" of length four, so store "()()".

Step 5: The result is "(())" and "()()", the two valid combinations for N equal to two.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Balanced Parentheses generates all valid combinations of N pairs of parentheses using backtracking. I build the string one character at a time while tracking how many opens and closes I have placed. I may append an open parenthesis whenever the open count is still below N, and I may append a close parenthesis only when the close count is strictly less than the open count. That close rule is the essential invariant, because it guarantees that no prefix ever has more closes than opens, so every string I build is valid without any after-the-fact checking. When the length reaches two times N I record a complete combination.

The reason I prefer this generate-and-prune approach over generating all possible strings and filtering is that it never builds an invalid prefix, so it does no wasted work. I also note that the number of valid combinations is the Catalan number, which grows quickly, so N must stay modest.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate valid nested approval structures, where a sub-approval can only open inside an open parent and every child must close before its parent, so for a given number of levels governance could review all valid workflow shapes. I backtracked with open and close counters so every generated structure was valid by construction. Explaining the two placement rules and why they keep every prefix valid is what shows an interviewer that I understand backtracking with invariants, not just brute-force enumeration.
